title: Don't Throw Ed Tech Babies Out With the Bathwater
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler writes from inside the skeptical camp, granting that the backlash against classroom technology is earned, and then argues that a blanket ban would discard the small number of tools that genuinely help. Her sorting principle is cognitive: learning requires effort, so any device that takes over the effort takes over the learning, which means student-facing tools deserve far more suspicion than teacher-facing ones. On the teacher side she describes Judy, a tool from The Writing Revolution trained on the Hochman Method that generates writing activities tied to whatever content a class is studying, and notes tools that produce decodable texts so beginning readers get practice on connected text. Student-facing tools can work if they question rather than answer, but she is candid that students are poorly motivated to use effortful tools and skilled at defeating safeguards, citing a reporter who got around a refusal simply by asking for an example essay. She treats the New York City and Los Angeles pauses as defensible temporary measures while districts inventory what is actually in use. The extended case study is Amira, a reading screener whose broad training makes it less likely than other computerized systems to misclassify bilingual students and non-standard accents as dyslexic.
points: Proposes a single sorting rule for ed tech, that any tool which absorbs the cognitive effort also absorbs the learning, which makes student-facing tools far riskier than teacher-facing ones.
Points to Judy from The Writing Revolution as a specialized tool that generates curriculum-matched writing activities while still requiring a teacher who knows the method to check the output.
Concedes the practical weakness of well-designed student tools, since effortful tools are unmotivating and students routinely talk generative models past their own refusals.
Treats the New York City and Los Angeles pauses as reasonable stopgaps for taking inventory, while warning that bans which do not distinguish helpful from harmful uses hold students back.
Uses Amira to show a concrete accuracy gain, since its wide training lets it tell a Spanish speaker's transposed pronunciation apart from a genuine misreading that other screeners flag as dyslexia.
quotes: A backlash against technology in the classroom is sweeping the country, part of a general wave of alarm about data centers, screen addiction, privacy, and the risk that unfettered access to generative AI will lead to a decline in students’ cognitive abilities.

Still, there are uses of technology, and of AI in particular, that can actually improve teaching and learning rather than undermining it. And a blanket call to rid classrooms of technology could sweep those beneficial uses out the door along with the pernicious ones.
It helps to understand, as I’ve argued before, that some cognitive effort is essential to learning—and that subcontracting out that effort to a device will also subcontract out the learning.
That suggests that we need to be much more cautious about student-facing technology than about technology used by teachers. Students, by definition, are in school to learn.
But students are likely to be less motivated to use a tool that requires them to expend effort, and they’re often adept at getting around whatever safeguards have been built in.

That may make sense as a temporary measure, giving officials time to identify what AI tools are being used in classrooms and evaluate the evidence behind them and the safeguards they incorporate. But bans of tech or AI that fail to distinguish between helpful and harmful uses can end up holding students back.

One problem with those systems is that they’re often biased against non-native English speakers or children with non-standard accents, erroneously identifying them as dyslexic—with potentially life-altering consequences.

Amira is able to recognize that the child is simply transposing Spanish pronunciation into English. But in the same sentence, the child reads the word her as here. Amira flags that misreading, which doesn’t align with the rules of Spanish pronunciation, as a true problem.
